# 7segment-demo

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A comparison tool for LED-style digit displays on the PicoCalc's 320x320
LCD, built on the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK. Author: Thomas Dzubin.

It exists to answer one question before a future project commits to a
look: *how big/bold/slanted should the digits be?* There are two entirely
separate screens - a **7-segment** one and a **14-segment** (alphanumeric)
one - since a real project uses one or the other, never both; `F1` swaps
between them. Every sample on either screen shows the same full glyph
(every segment, and the decimal point, lit), so each row or column is a
pure size/style comparison, not a comparison of which character is shown.

- **SIZE SWEEP** (top), smallest to largest:
  - 7-segment: six tiers from a bare-minimum 5x8px digit up to 34x56px
    (sized so eight digits span the 320px-wide screen: 8 x 34 + 7 x 6px
    gaps = 314px).
  - 14-segment: four tiers, 16x24 up to 40x64px. Fewer, larger tiers than
    the 7-segment screen - a 14-segment glyph's diagonals need much more
    room relative to segment thickness than straight bars do, so the same
    5x8-scale minimum just isn't legible here (see CHANGELOG.md).
- **STYLE SWEEP** (bottom): five looks at one shared size (26x42 for
  7-segment, 30x48 for 14-segment), so only the segment *shape* differs:
  `BLOCK` (baseline), `THIN`, `BOLD`, `ITALIC` (slanted, like a real LED
  clock), and `CHAMFER` (bevelled corners).

The 7-segment glyph is the classic `a..g` layout. The 14-segment glyph is
the same layout with the top, middle and bottom bars each split in two
(`a1/a2`, `g1/g2`, `d1/d2`), plus four diagonals connecting each corner to
the centre - which is what lets it form letters as well as digits.

## Controls

Size and style are two independent selections, each with its own highlight
box in the grid:

| Key           | Action                                                        |
|---------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| UP / DOWN     | move the SIZE selection (wraps)                                |
| LEFT / RIGHT  | move the STYLE selection (wraps)                                |
| ENTER         | tile the *combination* - the selected style, at the selected size tier's own w/h/thickness - edge-to-edge across the whole screen |
| ESC           | (from that detail view) back to the grid; from a grid, leave for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu |
| Q             | leave for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu, from any screen         |
| F1            | switch between the 7-segment and 14-segment screens             |
| ~ (SHIFT + `) | reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode, from any screen           |

Since the two selections are independent, ENTER can show any of the 30
size x style combinations on a screen, not just the 11 samples the grid
itself draws. Each screen remembers its own size/style selection
separately, so switching with `F1` and back returns you to where you left
off on the other one.

## Files

- `main.c` - `main()` and the selection/toggle/BOOTSEL key logic only.
- `sevenseg.c` / `sevenseg.h` - the reusable 7-segment drawing engine
  (`seg7_draw`, `seg7_draw_chamfered`, `seg7_draw_italic`, plus a digit ->
  segment-mask table). This is the part meant to be copied whole into a
  future project that wants a 7-segment-style readout.
- `seg14.c` / `seg14.h` - the reusable 14-segment drawing engine
  (`seg14_draw`, `seg14_draw_chamfered`, `seg14_draw_italic`), likewise
  meant to be copied whole into a future alphanumeric-readout project.
- `demo.c` / `demo.h` - the 7-segment screen's layout, built on `sevenseg.h`.
- `demo14.c` / `demo14.h` - the 14-segment screen's layout, built on
  `seg14.h`. Structurally identical to `demo.c` (same five styles, same
  controls) but with its own, larger size tiers and style-row reference
  size - see the SIZE SWEEP note above.
- `constants.h` - every tunable value, colour and layout position, shared
  by both screens (they're never shown at once, so they share the same
  screen real estate).
- `drivers/` - the LCD, keyboard and south-bridge drivers from
  [picocalc-text-starter](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
  by Blair Leduc, copied in verbatim (no audio driver - this demo has no
  sound).
- `CMakeLists.txt`, `pico_sdk_import.cmake` - firmware build config.
- `desktop/` - Desktop (SDL2) build for Windows and Linux: its own `CMakeLists.txt` plus a small shim of the
  driver API (no audio - this demo has no sound).
- `CHANGELOG.md` - notable changes, by version.

## Building

VS Code Pico extension (Compile / Run), or from a terminal with
`PICO_SDK_PATH` set:

    cmake -B build -G Ninja
    ninja -C build

Output: `build/7segment-demo-<chip>.uf2` (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or `RP2040`, matching the board). Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2` drive -
hold BOOTSEL on power-up, or press `~` (SHIFT + backtick) in the app.
The build also copies the `.uf2` to the top-level folder as
`7segment-demo-RP2350.uf2` / `7segment-demo-RP2040.uf2` (by board), so both
chips' builds sit side by side.

### Windows

The same program also runs on Windows through a small SDL2 layer in
[`desktop/`](desktop/) that stands in for the PicoCalc's LCD and keyboard.
From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2 installed:

    cmake -S desktop -B build-windows -G Ninja
    ninja -C build-windows

Output: `7segment-demo-Windows.exe` in the top-level folder. SDL2 is linked
statically, so it is a single file with no `SDL2.dll`. `~` simply closes the
program.

### Linux

The same source builds on Linux with the SDL2 development package installed
(for example `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`). Unlike the Windows build, SDL2 is
**not** linked in statically: the program links `libSDL2` dynamically, and the
build copies that library next to the executable as `libSDL2-2.0.so.0`, where
the executable finds it through an `$ORIGIN` run-path. Keep the two files
together.

    cmake -S desktop -B build-linux
    cmake --build build-linux

Output: `7segment-demo-Linux` and `libSDL2-2.0.so.0` in the top-level folder.

## License

MIT, see `LICENSE`. The vendored drivers from `picocalc-text-starter` by Blair Leduc keep their own license (see the `LICENSE` file that comes with them). They are his code of 2026-10-18 (commit `85a002e`) with two local changes: `lcd_putstr()` in `lcd.c` cuts a string
off at the right edge of the display, and `keyboard.c` treats a held key as a press, so that the arrow keys auto-repeat.
